title: Open model differentiation claims framework
summary: Working draft: concise claims framework for how we position 'verified profiles' for open models in the catalog. Includes what counts as evidence, competitive counters, sales-ready snippets, and open questions for product and research. Aim is to make a repeatable, lightweight playbook sales and marketing can use without overpromising.
audience: GTM (growth + sales enablement), product marketing, solutions engineering
background: We've gotten repeated asks from prospects who like open models for cost/flexibility but worry about variability: which model to pick, how to trust latency/cost/quality claims, and how to operationalize. We need a set of crisp, defensible claims tied to minimal evidence (so we can scale verification) and a set of competitor counters to use in conversations.
objectives: Define 4–6 standardized claims any 'verified profile' can make
Define the minimum evidence per claim (benchmarks, evals, provenance)
Create short sales snippets and technical follow-ups for common objections
Surface product gaps that block scaling verification automation
core_claims_framework: Claim A — Verified Performance Envelope: We publish 50/90/99 latency and throughput on Redwood serving for canonical sequence lengths and batch sizes; includes hardware spec and quantization mode.
Claim B — Production Quality Profile: Pass/fail on a small reproducible eval suite for common failure modes (hallucination, instruction-following, code correctness for code models).
Claim C — Versioned Behavior Snapshot: We publish model-weights identifier + tokenization spec + a small sample prompt/response snapshot so customers can detect regressions between versions.
Claim D — Provenance & Usage Constraints: Clear lineage (model repo + license), known data caveats, and suggested guardrails (temperature, max tokens, prompt patterns) for safe use.
Claim E — Cost/Performance Tradeoff Guidance: For typical workload archetypes (chat, completion, embeddings) we recommend model variants and quantization knobs with expected token-cost deltas.
Claim F — Fallback Compatibility: Specify a compatible fallback variant (e.g., fp16 -> int8 or larger -> smaller model) with measured quality delta so routing policies can use it safely.
minimum_evidence_matrix: Performance Envelope = microbench (p50/p90/p99), e2e request sample (cold/warm), hardware & runtime config, measurement date
Production Quality = small canonical eval set (20–50 prompts) + aggregated metrics (exact match, instr-following score, hallucination flag examples) + failure-mode notes
Versioned Snapshot = model-commit/sha, tokenizer version, 3 canonical prompt/response pairs saved, and a published diff note when updating
Provenance = link to upstream model repo, license text snippet, any fine-tuning dataset high-level description (no PII)
Cost Guidance = tokenized cost per 1k tokens per mode, recommended quantization options and expected latency/cost multipliers
Fallback Compatibility = validated smaller/quantized variant with measured quality regression (n points) and a compatibility list
evidence_examples_to_collect: Perf run: qps=75, p90=210ms for 512 tokens on a T4-8x pool, artifacts: perf-log-2025-02-05.csv
Eval run: 30 instruction prompts, IFR (instruction-follow rate) = 92%, 3 labeled hallucination examples
competitor_notes_and_counters: BigAPI (public LLM provider): Strength = polished consumer docs and simple pricing; Weakness = opaque serving stack and no per-customer versioned performance. Counter = emphasize our versioned snapshots and per-model serving profiles that map to predictable unit economics.

Cloud-managed endpoints (hyperscalers): Strength = deep infra and global regions; Weakness = limited curated open-model catalog and higher per-token overhead for small workloads. Counter = highlight our catalog curation and optimized runtime for predictable latency/cost on common sequence-length distributions.

Self-hosted runtimes from OSS vendors: Strength = control and low marginal infra cost; Weakness = ops burden and no standardized verification. Counter = call out Redwood's verification as a product feature: we operationalize the tests so customers don't re-run them internally.

Inference startups with microbench claims: Strength = strong latency-focused benchmarks; Weakness = often narrow model support and inconsistent evals. Counter = we combine latency benchmarks with quality evals and provenance so customers can trade cost vs quality with confidence.
sales_snippets_and_playbook_bullets: Snippet (discovery): 'Are you evaluating open models to reduce token costs or to control behavior? We can show side-by-side verified profiles that make both cost and quality tradeoffs explicit.'

Snippet (objection: trust): 'Instead of trusting a vendor claim, we give you a reproducible snapshot: model commit, tokenizer, 3 exact prompt/response pairs, and a short eval suite you can run in your environment.'
Technical follow-up (SE): 'If they want to validate, give them the perf artifact + eval bundle and run it on their traffic sample; we have a template runbook for that.'
Pricing angle: 'For customers with steady throughput, Redwood Dedicated lets you lock the verified profile to a fixed runtime and SLAs — so the published envelope becomes a contractual SLO.'
risks_product_gaps: Automation gap: verification currently requires manual bench runs and human review for hallucination labeling — needs more infra to scale to 100s of models.
Staleness risk: model snapshots decay — we need a refresh cadence and automated listeners for upstream model updates.
Legal/License complexity: some upstream models have ambiguous licenses or use restricted datasets; we need a legal sign-off step in the verification pipeline.
Quantization validity: not all quality evals transfer across quantization modes; we need separate evidence sets per quant mode.
open_questions_for_research_and_product: What is the minimal eval set that balances signal vs run-cost? (20 prompts? 50?)
What's the refresh cadence for a verified profile before it is flagged stale? (30/90/180 days)
Do we publish raw evaluation inputs/outputs or only aggregated metrics to avoid licensing/provenance noise?
Can we automate a 'compatibility test' that flags fallback variants with unacceptable regressions?
next_steps: GTM: build 3 sales one-pagers using the text snippets above for chat, embeddings, and code workloads
Product: proposal for verification automation (INF-7892) due next week
Research: prototype minimal eval set on 10 candidate open models and share results
Legal: quick review of 20 highest-requested open-model licenses
notes_to_self: Keep this lightweight — aim for a single-page public-facing 'verified profile' header + a hidden deeper artifact for SEs. Iterate after 10 customer trials.
